title: Rumi's tomb
hookLine: in Konya, his tomb is visited by people of many backgrounds
tomorrow: a survivor's prayers. why would anyone call them psalms?

cards: Flowers left at a gate. Candles outside a venue after a singer dies. Notes taped to a wall by people who never met the person.
Saying goodbye to someone you only knew through their words is its own kind of grief. For Rumi, there's a place to go.

In Konya, in Turkey, his tomb stands under a tiled dome, and people come: Muslims, and visitors of many backgrounds, some who've read every line and some who know one. So where would you go to say goodbye to Rumi? There.

teach.b: Aflaki, who wrote down stories of Rumi's circle, tells of his funeral: tradition says Christians and Jews walked with the Muslims behind the bier, weeping, each saying in their own way that he had taught them something.
Whatever the details, the scene has stuck to the place. The welcome is still part of it.
A verse is hung near the tomb and printed on cards: come, come again, whoever you are, even if you've broken your promise again and again, come. Here's the honest part.
Some scholars of Persian poetry say the verse isn't found in Rumi's own works, and trace it to an earlier poet. It may not be his.

teach.h: MAYBE NOT HIS. STILL HIS DOOR.
teach.b: But it has become his door, and it says something the Qur'an says first: don't despair of God's mercy, because He forgives. Coming back is always allowed. That's what the tomb gives a person this week.
Maybe you've drifted. Maybe it's been a long time since you prayed, or went to the masjid, or opened the book. Maybe you feel like a fraud walking back in.
The door at Konya, and the verse on it, say the same thing a door of mercy says: you're not too late, and you're not the first.

how: Visitors to Rumi's tomb in Konya, now a museum, file past his sarcophagus; Muslims among them recite al-Fatiha or ask mercy for him, and others stand in silence.

games.q: your cousin stopped praying for a year. Eid is coming, and she says she'd feel like a hypocrite at the prayer. what fits today?
o: come anyway; the door says come again, however long it's been.
wait until she's back to praying daily, so she's not a fraud.
stay home; Eid prayer is for people who never stopped.
games.why: the Qur'an says don't despair of God's mercy, and the verse at Konya says come again. coming back is always allowed.

practice: If you pray, ask mercy for Rumi in whatever words come; Muslims say rahimahullah, may God have mercy on him, after the name of someone who has died.
Or say aloud the name of one teacher, living or gone, whose words still reach you, and thank them out loud.

wordCard.voice: Rumi's tomb: his resting place in Konya, where people of many backgrounds come, and a verse at the door says come again.

orig.note: Arabic: may God have mercy on him; said after the name of a man who has died.

carryVoice: For anyone who's been away a while: come, come again, however long it's been. All eight of Rumi's stories, told.
